patient.chief_complaint: Brought by roommates - continuous generalized convulsions for 20 minutes, no stopping
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Allen is a 32-year-old man with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy on valproic acid who is brought by ambulance after his roommates found him in a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that did not stop. The seizure began approximately 20 minutes prior to EMS arrival. He had been awake and appeared his normal self earlier that morning. His roommates are not aware of whether he took his medication last night or this morning. He had worked a late shift at the bar last night and drank significant alcohol afterward. He appears to have had only 3-4 hours of sleep. He has no known prior episodes of status epilepticus. His JME was diagnosed at age 17 and has been incompletely controlled on valproate due to inconsistent medication adherence. He has had several breakthrough seizures over the years, typically associated with sleep deprivation and alcohol use, which are well-known triggers for JME. On EMS arrival he was in continuous generalized tonic-clonic activity. Paramedics administered diazepam 10 mg IV en route without termination of seizures. He arrives to the ED in active status epilepticus, still convulsing.

output.query: Status epilepticus treatment protocol JME valproate subtherapeutic rhabdomyolysis management

results.finding: SE treatment algorithm: Benzodiazepine first (lorazepam or diazepam) → IV AED (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate) → anesthesia if refractory
JME: valproate remains preferred AED - ethosuximide or levetiracetam alternatives
SE with rhabdomyolysis: aggressive IV hydration target UO 1-2 mL/kg/h; myoglobinuria prevention
Alcohol + JME: seizure risk highest during acute intoxication and withdrawal phase 24-48h
SE prevention: consistent AED adherence; avoid alcohol; prioritize sleep in JME

output.summary: SE management in idiopathic generalized epilepsy: benzodiazepine as first-line; IV valproate preferred for JME over phenytoin, which may worsen myoclonic components. Rhabdomyolysis complicating SE: aggressive IV hydration targeting urine output 1–2 mL/kg/h. Evidence supports medication adherence and trigger avoidance (sleep deprivation, alcohol) as primary SE prevention strategies in JME.

output.query: Rhabdomyolysis seizure status epilepticus CK management acute kidney injury prevention

results.finding: CK >5000 U/L associated with higher AKI risk in rhabdomyolysis
Aggressive IV hydration: isotonic saline at 200-1000 mL/h targeting UO 1-2 mL/kg/h
Urine dipstick for myoglobinuria - blood positive without RBCs on microscopy
Monitor BUN/Cr every 6-8h during first 24h of rhabdomyolysis
Bicarbonate alkalinization controversial but used in severe cases

output.summary: Rhabdomyolysis from seizures: CK elevation above 5000 U/L is associated with higher acute kidney injury risk. Aggressive IV hydration with isotonic saline targeting urine output 1–2 mL/kg/h is standard management. Urine dipstick positive for blood without RBCs on microscopy suggests myoglobinuria. Serial CK and creatinine monitoring every 6–8 h recommended in the first 24 h.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
DaTscan / dopamine transporter imaging has no role in SE; no parkinsonism question relevant to acute management.

sequence_constraints.reason: Confirm pregnancy test before reloading valproate in any reproductive-age woman; here patient is male so soft constraint.

critical_actions: Administer IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg first-line — do not delay for diagnostics
IV valproate reload 30-40 mg/kg + IV levetiracetam — both first-line in JME per ESETT and JME-specific guidance
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT use phenytoin / fosphenytoin in JME — exacerbates myoclonus
Do NOT use carbamazepine / oxcarbazepine / gabapentin in JME
Do NOT discharge without addressing non-adherence
Avoid phenytoin/carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine/gabapentin in JME — can exacerbate myoclonus and worsen generalized seizures.
key_reasoning_points: JME is a generalized epilepsy where sodium-channel-blocking AEDs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) worsen myoclonus
Subtherapeutic valproate in non-adherent JME is a common SE trigger
Alcohol intake (still intoxicated) is contributory, not the primary cause
Post-convulsive lactic acidosis resolves spontaneously and does not require bicarbonate
